paragraphs: But Dmitri Fyodorovitch was speeding along the road. It was a little more than twenty versts to Mokroe, but Andrey’s three horses galloped so hard that the distance could be covered in an hour and a quarter. The swift motion revived Mitya. The air was fresh and cool, and big stars shone in the sky. It was the very night, and perhaps the very hour, when Alyosha threw himself on the earth and swore in rapture to love it forever and ever.

All was confusion, confusion, in Mitya’s soul. Many things were goading his heart, but at that moment his whole being yearned for her, his queen, to whom he was flying to look on her for the last time. One thing I can say for certain: his heart did not waver for a single instant. I may not be believed when I say that this jealous lover felt not the slightest jealousy of the new rival, who seemed to have sprung out of the earth. If any other man had appeared, he would have been jealous at once, and might have stained his fierce hands with blood again. But as he flew through the night, he felt no envy, not even any hostility, toward the man who had been her first lover.... It is true he had not yet seen him.

“Here there was no room for dispute: it was her right and his. This was her first love, and after five years she had not forgotten it. So she had loved him all those five years, and I—how do I come into it? What right have I? Step aside, Mitya, and make way! What am I now? Now everything is over except for the officer—even if he had not appeared, everything would be over ...”

These words would roughly have expressed his feelings, if he had been able to reason. But he could not reason at that moment. His present plan had not come from reasoning. It had sprung from feeling at Fenya’s first words, and he had adopted it in a flash, with all its consequences. And yet, despite his resolution, there was confusion in his soul, an agonizing confusion: his resolution gave him no peace. So much lay behind him that tortured him. And at moments it seemed strange to him that he had written his own death sentence with pen and paper—“I punish myself”—and that the paper was lying there in his pocket, ready; the pistol was loaded; and he had already decided how, next morning, he would greet the first warm ray of “golden-haired Phœbus.”

And yet he could not be rid of the past, of all he had left behind, which tortured him. He felt this miserably, and the thought of it sank into his heart with despair. There was one moment when he felt an impulse to stop Andrey, jump out of the cart, pull out his loaded pistol and make an end of everything without waiting for the dawn. But that moment flew by like a spark. The horses galloped on, “devouring space,” and as he drew near his goal, the thought of her, of her alone, took fuller and fuller possession of his soul again, chasing away the fearful images that had haunted it. Oh, how he longed to look at her, if only for a moment, if only from a distance!

“She’s with _him_ now,” he thought. “Now I’ll see what she looks like with him, her first love, and that’s all I want.” Never had this woman, who had such a fateful influence on his life, stirred such love in his breast, such a new and unknown feeling, surprising even to himself, a feeling tender to the point of devotion, to the point of self-effacement before her! “I will efface myself!” he said, in a rush of almost hysterical ecstasy.

They had been galloping for nearly an hour. Mitya was silent, and Andrey, though usually a talkative peasant, had not said a word either. He seemed afraid to talk. He only whipped up his three lean but spirited bay horses. Suddenly Mitya cried out in horrible anxiety:
“Andrey! What if they’re asleep?”
The thought fell on him like a blow. It had not occurred to him before.
“They may well have gone to bed by now, Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”
Mitya frowned as if in pain. Yes, indeed ... he was rushing there ... with such feelings ... while they were asleep ... she was asleep, perhaps, there too.... An angry feeling surged up in his heart.
“Drive on, Andrey! Whip them up! Look alive!” he cried, beside himself.
“But maybe they’re not in bed!” Andrey went on after a pause. “Timofey said there was a crowd of them there—”
“At the station?”
“Not at the posting-station, but at Plastunov’s, the inn, where they hire out horses, too.”
“I know it. So you say there are a lot of them? How’s that? Who are they?” cried Mitya, greatly dismayed at this unexpected news.
“Well, Timofey said they’re all gentlefolk. Two from our town—I can’t say who—and two others, strangers, maybe more besides. I didn’t ask particularly. They’ve sat down to cards, Timofey said.”
“Cards?”
“So maybe they’re not in bed, if they’re at cards. It’s likely not even eleven yet.”
“Faster, Andrey! Faster!” Mitya cried again, nervously.
“May I ask you something, sir?” said Andrey, after a pause. “Only I’m afraid of making you angry, sir.”
“What is it?”

“Well, Fenya threw herself at your feet just now and begged you not to harm her mistress, and someone else, too ... so you see, sir— I’m the one taking you there ... forgive me, sir, it’s my conscience ... maybe it’s stupid of me to speak of it—”
Mitya suddenly seized him by the shoulders from behind.
“Are you a driver?” he asked frantically.
“Yes, sir.”

“Then you know that a man has to make way. What would you say about a driver who wouldn’t make way for anyone, but just drove on and crushed people? No, a driver mustn’t run people over. You can’t run over a man. You can’t spoil people’s lives. And if you have spoiled a life—punish yourself.... If only you’ve spoiled, if only you’ve ruined anyone’s life—punish yourself and go away.”
These words burst from Mitya almost hysterically. Andrey was surprised at him, but he kept up the conversation.

“That’s right, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, you’re quite right. One mustn’t crush or torment a man, or any creature, for every creature is made by God. Take a horse, for instance. Some folks, even among us drivers, drive any old way. Nothing will hold them back, they just force it along.”

“To hell?” Mitya interrupted, and burst into his abrupt, short laugh. “Andrey, simple soul,” he seized him by the shoulders again, “tell me, will Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov go to hell or not, what do you think?”

“I don’t know, darling, it depends on you, for you are ... you see, sir, when the Son of God was nailed to the Cross and died, He went straight down to hell from the Cross and set free all the sinners who were in agony. And the devil groaned, because he thought he would get no more sinners in hell. And God said to him then, ‘Don’t groan, for you shall have all the mighty of the earth, the rulers, the chief judges and the rich men, and you shall be filled up as you have been in all the ages till I come again.’ Those were His very words ...”
“A peasant legend! Splendid! Whip up the left one, Andrey!”

“So you see, sir, who hell is for,” said Andrey, whipping up the left horse, “but you’re like a little child ... that’s how we look on you ... and though you’re quick-tempered, sir, God will forgive you for your kind heart.”
“And you, do you forgive me, Andrey?”
“What should I forgive you for, sir? You’ve never done me any harm.”
“No, for everyone, for everyone, you here alone, on the road—will you forgive me for everyone? Speak, simple peasant heart!”
“Oh, sir! I’m getting afraid to drive you, your talk is so strange.”
But Mitya did not hear. He was praying frantically and muttering to himself.

“Lord, receive me, with all my lawlessness, and do not condemn me. Let me pass by Your judgment ... do not condemn me, for I have condemned myself. Do not condemn me, for I love You, O Lord. I am a wretch, but I love You. If You send me to hell, I shall love You there, and from there I shall cry out that I love You forever and ever.... But let me love to the end.... Here and now, for just five hours ... till the first light of Your day ... for I love the queen of my soul ... I love her and I cannot help loving her. You see my whole heart.... I shall gallop up, I shall fall before her and say, ‘You are right to pass on and leave me. Farewell, and forget your victim ... never fret yourself about me!’”
“Mokroe!” cried Andrey, pointing ahead with his whip.

Through the pale darkness of the night loomed a solid black mass of buildings, flung down, as it were, on the vast plain. The village of Mokroe had two thousand inhabitants, but at that hour all were asleep, and only here and there a few lights still twinkled.
“Drive on, Andrey, I’m coming!” Mitya exclaimed feverishly.
“They’re not asleep,” said Andrey again, pointing with his whip to the Plastunovs’ inn, at the entrance to the village. The six windows facing the street were all brightly lit.
“They’re not asleep,” Mitya repeated joyfully. “Faster, Andrey! Gallop! Drive up with a dash! Set the bells ringing! Let everyone know I’ve come. I’m coming! I’m coming, too!”
Andrey lashed his exhausted team into a gallop, drove up with a dash and pulled up his steaming, panting horses at the high flight of steps.
Mitya jumped out of the cart just as the innkeeper, on his way to bed, peeped out from the steps, curious to see who had arrived.
“Trifon Borissovitch, is that you?”
The innkeeper bent down, peered at him, ran down the steps and rushed up to his guest with fawning delight.
“Dmitri Fyodorovitch, your honor! Do I see you again?”

Trifon Borissovitch was a thickset, healthy peasant of middle height, with a rather fat face. His expression was severe and uncompromising, especially with the peasants of Mokroe, but he could put on the most fawning look when he sensed it was to his advantage. He dressed in Russian style, in a shirt buttoned down one side and a full-skirted coat. He had saved a good sum of money but was forever dreaming of improving his position. More than half the peasants were in his clutches, and everyone in the neighborhood was in debt to him. From the neighboring landowners he bought and rented land, which the peasants worked in payment of debts they could never shake off. He was a widower with four grown-up daughters. One of them was already a widow and lived in the inn with her two children, his grandchildren, and worked for him like a charwoman. Another daughter was married to a petty official, and in one of the rooms of the inn, among the family photographs on the wall, you could see a miniature photograph of this official in uniform and official epaulettes. The two younger daughters wore fashionable blue or green dresses, tight at the back, with trains a yard long, on Church holidays or when they went visiting. But next morning they would get up at dawn as usual, sweep out the rooms with a birch broom, empty the slops and clean up after the lodgers.

In spite of the thousands of roubles he had saved, Trifon Borissovitch was very fond of emptying the pockets of a drunken guest. He remembered that not a month ago he had made two, if not three, hundred roubles out of Dmitri in twenty-four hours, when Dmitri came on his escapade with Grushenka. So now he met him with eager welcome, scenting his prey the moment Mitya drove up to the steps.
“Dmitri Fyodorovitch, dear sir, we see you once more!”
“Wait, Trifon Borissovitch,” began Mitya, “first and foremost, where is she?”
“Agrafena Alexandrovna?” The innkeeper understood at once, looking sharply into Mitya’s face. “She’s here, too ...”
“With whom? With whom?”

“Some strangers. One is an official gentleman, a Pole, to judge by his speech. He sent the horses for her from here. And there’s another with him, a friend of his or a fellow traveler, there’s no telling. They’re dressed as civilians.”
“Well, are they feasting? Have they money?”
“Poor sort of feast! Nothing to boast of, Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”
“Nothing to boast of? And who are the others?”

“They’re two gentlemen from the town.... They’ve come back from Tcherny and are staying here. One’s quite a young gentleman, a relative of Mr. Miüsov, he must be, but I’ve forgotten his name ... and I expect you know the other one too, a gentleman called Maximov. He’s been on a pilgrimage, so he says, to the monastery in the town. He’s traveling with this young relation of Mr. Miüsov.”
“Is that all?”
“Yes.”
“Wait, listen, Trifon Borissovitch. Tell me the main thing: what about her? How is she?”
“Oh, she’s only just arrived. She’s sitting with them.”
“Is she cheerful? Is she laughing?”
“No, I think she’s not laughing much. She’s sitting there quite dull. She’s combing the young gentleman’s hair.”
“The Pole—the officer?”
“He’s not young, and he’s not an officer, either. Not him, sir. It’s the young gentleman who’s Mr. Miüsov’s relation ... I’ve forgotten his name.”
“Kalganov.”
“That’s it, Kalganov!”
“All right. I’ll see for myself. Are they playing cards?”
“They were playing, but they’ve stopped. They’ve been drinking tea, and the official gentleman asked for liqueurs.”
“Wait, Trifon Borissovitch, wait, my good soul, I’ll see for myself. Now answer one more question: are the gypsies here?”

“You can’t have the gypsies now, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. The authorities have sent them away. But we’ve got Jews in the village who play the cymbals and the fiddle, so one could send for them. They’d come.”
“Send for them. By all means send for them!” cried Mitya. “And you can get the girls together as you did then, Marya especially, and Stepanida, and Arina, too. Two hundred roubles for a chorus!”

“Oh, for a sum like that I can get the whole village together, though they’re asleep by now. Are the peasants here worth such kindness, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, or the girls either? To spend a sum like that on such coarse, rude people! What’s the good of giving a peasant a cigar to smoke, the stinking ruffian! And the girls are all lousy. Besides, I’ll get my daughters up for nothing, let alone for a sum like that. They’ve only just gone to bed—I’ll give them a kick and set them singing for you. You gave the peasants champagne to drink the other day, e—ech!”

For all his pretended compassion for Mitya, Trifon Borissovitch had hidden half a dozen bottles of champagne on that last occasion, and had picked up a hundred-rouble note under the table, which had stayed in his clutches.
“Trifon Borissovitch, I sent more than a thousand flying last time I was here. Do you remember?”
“You did send it flying. I certainly remember. You must have left three thousand behind you.”
“Well, I’ve come to do the same again, you see?”
And he pulled out his roll of notes and held them up under the innkeeper’s nose.

“Now listen and remember. In an hour the wine will arrive, with savories, pies and sweets—bring them all up at once. That box Andrey has got is to be brought up at once, too. Open it, and serve champagne immediately. And the girls, we must have the girls, Marya especially.”
He turned to the cart and pulled out the box of pistols.
“Here, Andrey, let’s settle up. Here’s fifteen roubles for the drive, and fifty for vodka ... for your readiness, for your love.... Remember Karamazov!”
“I’m afraid, sir,” faltered Andrey. “Give me five roubles extra, but I won’t take more. Trifon Borissovitch, bear witness. Forgive my foolish words ...”

“What are you afraid of?” asked Mitya, studying him. “Well, go to the devil, if that’s it!” he cried, flinging him five roubles. “Now, Trifon Borissovitch, take me up quietly and let me get a look at them first, without being seen. Where are they? In the blue room?”

Trifon Borissovitch looked at Mitya uneasily, but at once did his bidding obediently. He led him into the passage, went himself into the first large room, next to the one where the visitors were sitting, and took the light away. Then he stealthily led Mitya in and put him in a dark corner, from where he could watch the company freely without being seen. But Mitya did not look long. In fact he could not see them at all; he saw her. His heart throbbed violently, and all went dark before his eyes.

She was sitting sideways to the table in a low chair, and beside her on the sofa sat the pretty youth, Kalganov. She was holding his hand and seemed to be laughing, while he, looking vexed and not looking at her, was saying something in a loud voice to Maximov, who sat on the other side of the table, facing Grushenka. Maximov was laughing violently at something. On the sofa sat _he_, and on a chair by the sofa sat the other stranger. The one on the sofa was lolling backwards, smoking a pipe, and Mitya had an impression of a stoutish, broad-faced, short little man who was apparently angry about something. His friend, the other stranger, struck Mitya as extraordinarily tall, but he could make out nothing more. He caught his breath. He could not bear it for a minute. He put the pistol-case on a chest and, with a throbbing heart and a cold feeling all over, walked straight into the blue room to face the company.
“Aie!” shrieked Grushenka, the first to notice him.
